papers_read.title_as_printed: The Role of Vitamin E in Slowing Down Mild Cognitive Impairment: A Narrative Review (Lakhan, Sharma, Batra, Beatty; Healthcare 2021, 9, 1573)
Oxidative Stress in Brain in Amnestic Mild Cognitive Impairment (Butterfield; Antioxidants 2023, 12, 462)

what_each_reports.P-1196: Narrative review of 22 studies (7 animal, 15 human) from ~2010-2021; no pooled estimate ('restricted our ability to generate pooled estimates'). Vote count: abstract says 11 studies showed some neuroprotective effect; results text says 6/7 animal and 8/15 human (=14); Table 2 column totals sum to 23 for n = 22. Its Conclusions state that no study type has 'provided the conclusive answer' on whether vitamin E slows MCI progression. The Discussion nonetheless suggests annual checks of vitamin E levels in the elderly and supplementation 'in maintaining its adequate level', and mentions 800-2000 IU/day as the range of reported SAFE doses (a toxicity ceiling, not a recommended dose). Its Table A1 includes Edmonds et al. 2018 (756 MCI, donepezil vs vitamin E) with the conclusion 'Vitamin E may not have an effect on lowering the rate of MCI towards AD'.
what_each_reports.P-1199: Mechanistic review of redox proteomics in MCI brain. Section 5 states that clinical antioxidant trials in AD and MCI 'have been for the most part quite disappointing' and describes one trial: a three-year double-blind trial of 769 MCI participants (placebo, 2000 IU vitamin E, 10 mg donepezil) in which 'Vitamin E demonstrated no improvement'. No systematic search, no effect estimate.

quantity_a: No estimand: a qualitative vote count across heterogeneous animal and human studies (various outcomes: cognition, oxidative markers, plasma tocopherol association) plus a clinical-practice suggestion; conclusion 'not conclusive'.
quantity_b: No estimand: a qualitative appraisal of antioxidant trials in MCI/AD, illustrated by one vitamin E trial (769 MCI, progression to AD over 3 years) reported as null.
incompatible_if_same: No. On the only shared object, the large vitamin E/donepezil MCI trial, both papers agree it was null (P-1196 tabulates its 756-participant secondary analysis as 'Vitamin E may not have an effect'; P-1199 reports 'no improvement'). P-1196's own conclusion ('inconclusive') is compatible with P-1199's 'mostly disappointing'. What remains is a practice suggestion in one paper, which is not a result.

gates.dataset_family: partial overlap: P-1196 pools 2010-2021 animal and human studies; P-1199 cites the ADCS vitamin E/donepezil MCI trial, which also appears in P-1196 via its secondary analysis (Edmonds 2018)
gates.modality_family: match at the level of intervention class (oral vitamin E/antioxidant), though P-1199's own subject is post-mortem proteomics

endpoint_and_metric: incompatible: neither paper reports a metric; P-1196's 'neuroprotective effect' mixes cognitive outcomes, oxidative markers and cross-sectional plasma associations, P-1199's appraisal concerns trial progression/cognition endpoints
independence: Distinct authors and venues; partial overlap in primary evidence (the ADCS MCI vitamin E/donepezil trial is represented in both).
grounds: P-1196's own conclusion is that the evidence is inconclusive, which is compatible with P-1199's appraisal that antioxidant trials were mostly disappointing.
On the one trial both papers address, they agree it showed no vitamin E benefit in MCI.

The record's claim that P-1196 'converts' the vote count into a dosing recommendation of 800-2000 IU/day misreads the paper: 800-2000 IU/day is quoted as the reported safe-dose range to avoid toxicity.
A clinical-practice suggestion set against a narrative appraisal is not two incompatible results on the same quantity; neither paper reports an effect estimate.

evidence_quotes.quote: In conclusion, epidemiological, clinical, nor other studies have provided the conclusive answer to whether or not Vitamin E slows the progression of MCI.

The guidelines on the safe dose of vitamin E varies from 800–2000 IU/day as reported by previous studies [46,47]. Therefore, these findings should be considered rather carefully to prevent any toxic effects of vitamin E.
It would be recommended for clinical practice that the Vitamin E levels be checked annually in the elderly, and they should be provided Vitamin E supplementation in maintaining its adequate level.
The effect of donepezil and Vitamin E was compared for 756 MCI participants. ... Vitamin E may not have an effect on lowering the rate of MCI towards AD.
The results were equivocal. Eleven studies showed some level of the neuroprotective effect of Vitamin E, tocopherols and tocotrienols on the progression of MCI.

out of seven, six studies ... exhibited some level of the neuroprotective effect ... out of 15 studies conducted on humans, eight studies reported Vitamin E's role in lowering the risk or delaying cognitive impairment.
clinical trials of antioxidants in AD and MCI have been for the most part quite disappointing [134,135].

A three-year, double-blind clinical trial involving 769 MCI participants treated daily with placebo, 2000 IU of vitamin E, or 10 mg of donepezil was conducted [136]. Vitamin E demonstrated no improvement in MCI patients

record_defects: claim_a and conflict_statement say P-1196 recommends supplementation 'at 800-2000 IU/day'; the PDF gives 800-2000 IU/day as the reported safe-dose range (toxicity ceiling), and the recommendation is supplementation to maintain adequate levels.

conflict_statement says P-1196 'concludes vitamin E has some neuroprotective role'; the paper's Conclusions section says no study type has provided a conclusive answer (the 'some neuroprotective effect' wording is in the Discussion).

claim_a's '11/22 studies ... (6/7 animal, 8/15 human)' conflates two non-reconciling counts in the PDF: the abstract says 11, the results text gives 6/7 + 8/15 = 14, and Table 2 totals sum to 23 for n = 22.

The record implies the evidence bases do not overlap at the 769-participant trial; P-1196 includes the same ADCS vitamin E/donepezil MCI trial via Edmonds et al. 2018 (756 MCI) and records it as null.
Registry codes P-1199 as study_design_type review_meta_analysis; it is a narrative mechanistic review with no search or synthesis of trials.
Minor: P-1196 tabulates Dysken 2014 (a trial in Alzheimer disease) as evidence on MCI progression; not load-bearing for this verdict.
what_would_change_the_verdict: Only a quantitative estimate in either paper of vitamin E's effect on MCI progression; neither provides one. If the operator treats P-1196's practice suggestion as a claim of efficacy, the pair would at most be documented_incommensurability (no shared estimand), not genuine.
